name: Hydrogen
tagline: The lightest atom: one proton, one electron, one hand. It holds exactly one partner.
atomStory: Hydrogen is the simplest atom. One proton (a tiny + particle) sits in the middle. One electron (a tiny − particle) goes around it. It has one hand, so it holds exactly one partner. That is why hydrogen caps the ends and sides of every hydrocarbon chain. It is so light that its molecules, and its engine exhaust, move faster than any heavier gas at the same temperature.

uses.title: Ammonia for fertilizer
uses.why: About a third of factory-made hydrogen is joined with nitrogen from air to make ammonia (NH3). Only refining uses more. Each hydrogen holds one of nitrogen's 3 hands.

uses.title: Cleaning fuels (hydrotreating)
uses.why: Refineries push hydrogen over catalysts (helpers that speed up a reaction). It pulls sulfur out of fuels as H2S and fills in shaky double bonds. With one hand, each hydrogen neatly caps one broken bond.

uses.title: Rocket fuel
uses.why: Liquid hydrogen burned with liquid oxygen gives the fastest exhaust of any common chemical rocket fuel pair, about 4.4 km/s in vacuum. The exhaust molecules are very light, so the same heat throws them out faster.

uses.title: Making methane (Sabatier)
uses.why: CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O, with nickel as the catalyst. Hydrogen fills carbon's 4 hands and carries the oxygens off as water.

bonds.name: Hydrogen gas
bonds.note: Two hydrogens hold hands, so neither has an empty hand. This is how hydrogen exists as a gas.

bonds.name: Water
bonds.note: Oxygen's 2 hands each hold one hydrogen. Water is the main product of burning any fuel that contains hydrogen.

bonds.name: Methane
bonds.note: Carbon's 4 hands each hold one hydrogen. The simplest hydrocarbon and Raptor's fuel.

bonds.name: Ammonia
bonds.note: Three hydrogens hold nitrogen's 3 hands. Nearly all nitrogen fertilizer starts here.

number.label: Density (weight for its size) of liquid hydrogen: about 1/14 of water and 1/6 of liquid methane

source: About three-quarters of the universe's ordinary matter by weight. On Earth it is locked in water and hydrocarbons. Industry mostly makes it by steam methane reforming (CH4 + H2O → CO + 3H2). Coal gasification is second. Only a small share comes from splitting water with electricity (electrolysis).

lenses.nexus: Polyethylene (CH2)n is about 14% hydrogen by weight. At your plant, pyrolysis has to split that hydrogen among its products. Gas and light oil get lots of it. Char is the carbon left behind after the hydrogen has gone elsewhere.
lenses.rocket: Hydrogen gives the fastest exhaust, but it is so light for its size that its tanks get huge. At -253 °C it boils off and leaks through tiny gaps. That trade-off is a big reason Starship chose methane instead.

name: Helium
tagline: The full, content gas: 2 electrons fill its only ring, so it has no hands. It reacts with nothing and stays a gas almost to absolute zero.
atomStory: Helium's one ring holds its limit of 2 electrons (tiny − particles). So it has no hands and nothing to bond with. Those 2 electrons sit very close to 2 protons (+ particles) in the middle. No other atom holds its electrons tighter. Helium atoms barely pull on each other, so it only turns liquid at -269 °C.

uses.title: Pushing propellant out of tanks
uses.why: Helium gas pushes propellant (fuel and oxidizer) out of the tanks toward the pumps. It is light, never reacts, and stays a gas even touching -183 °C liquid oxygen.

uses.title: MRI magnets
uses.why: Liquid helium chills MRI superconducting magnets to about 4 K (-269 °C). Nothing else stays liquid that cold.

uses.title: Leak detection
uses.why: Helium atoms are tiny and never react, so they slip through leaks other gases can't. Air has only about 5 parts per million of helium. So a detector picks up a leak easily.

uses.title: Balloons and airships
uses.why: Helium is about 7 times lighter than air. Unlike hydrogen, it cannot burn.

bonds.name: Helium hydride ion
bonds.note: Helium only bonds as a charged particle (an ion) like this. Scientists think it was the first molecule to form after the Big Bang.

number.label: Boiling point (4.2 K), the lowest of any element

source: Uranium and thorium in rock shoot out alpha particles, which are helium nuclei (atom centers). Over millions of years that helium collects in some natural gas fields. It is separated out by deep cooling.

lenses.rocket: Falcon 9 keeps helium in high-pressure composite bottles to pressurize its tanks. Starship reportedly uses autogenous pressurization instead: it taps heated methane and oxygen gas from its own engines. That removes most of the need for helium.

name: Lithium
tagline: The lightest metal: one loose outer electron it gives away easily, which makes it the go-to atom for batteries.
atomStory: Lithium has 2 electrons (tiny − particles) on an inner ring and just 1 on its outer ring. That outer one is held loosely. Lithium would rather give it away than hold hands. Then it becomes a tiny Li+ ion (a charged atom). Small, light, and eager to give away an electron: that is what a battery needs.

uses.title: Lithium-ion batteries
uses.why: The tiny Li+ ion shuttles between the battery's two ends (electrodes). Lithium's eagerness to give up its electron gives each cell a high voltage. Its standard electrode potential, -3.04 V, is the most negative of any element.

uses.title: Aluminum-lithium alloys
uses.why: In this metal mix, each 1% of lithium makes aluminum about 3% less dense and about 6% stiffer. The light lithium atoms form tiny Al3Li specks that stiffen the metal.

uses.title: CO2 scrubbers
uses.why: Lithium hydroxide soaks up CO2 in spacecraft and submarines. Lithium is so light that each kg carried removes a lot of CO2.

uses.title: Grease
uses.why: Most all-purpose grease is oil thickened with a lithium soap. It keeps its shape over a wide range of temperatures.

bonds.name: Lithium carbonate
bonds.note: The main form lithium is bought and sold in. It gets refined into battery cathode (+ side) materials.

bonds.name: Lithium hydroxide
bonds.note: A strong base (the opposite of an acid). Used for battery cathodes and to soak up CO2 (2LiOH + CO2 → Li2CO3 + H2O).

bonds.name: Lithium cobalt oxide
bonds.note: The classic Li-ion cathode. Lithium ions slip in and out between cobalt oxide layers as the battery charges and drains.

bonds.name: Lithium nitride
bonds.note: Lithium is the only alkali metal (the give-away column) that reacts with air's nitrogen at room temperature.

number.label: Density (weight for its size), about half of water: the lightest metal

source: Salty brine is pumped up and dried down in evaporation ponds on South American salt flats. Or it is mined from hard-rock minerals such as spodumene, mainly in Australia.

lenses.nexus: Butyllithium kicks off the chain reaction that links butadiene and styrene into synthetic rubbers. Its lithium-carbon bond is very lopsided, so the carbon carries a spare electron pair. That pair attacks the first monomer (single building block).
lenses.rocket: Falcon 9's propellant tanks are aluminum-lithium alloy. A little lithium buys lighter, stiffer tank walls. Apollo 13's crew survived on makeshift LiOH canisters that kept CO2 from building up.

name: Beryllium
tagline: The stiff featherweight: lighter than aluminum and about 40% stiffer than steel.
atomStory: Beryllium has 2 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring. The atom is small and they sit close to the center. So unlike most metals, it doesn't give them away freely. Its bonds are short and partly shared, like half-held hands. That makes the metal very stiff for its weight. It has only 4 electrons in all, so X-rays pass right through it.

uses.title: Space telescope mirrors
uses.why: JWST's 18 mirror segments are gold-coated beryllium. It is light, stiff, and holds its shape when chilled below -220 °C in space.

uses.title: X-ray windows
uses.why: Few electrons per atom means little to block X-rays. So thin beryllium sheets seal X-ray tubes and detectors and still let the beam through.

uses.title: Beryllium copper
uses.why: About 2% beryllium makes copper as strong as many steels. It still conducts and doesn't spark. That makes it ideal for springs, connectors and safety tools.

uses.title: Neutron reflectors
uses.why: Beryllium bounces neutrons (uncharged particles from atom centers) back into a reactor core and can release extra ones. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by firing alpha particles at beryllium.

bonds.name: Beryllium oxide
bonds.note: A ceramic that moves heat almost as well as some metals but blocks electricity. Its dust, like all beryllium dust, can cause a long-term lung disease.

bonds.name: Beryl
bonds.note: The mineral behind emerald (green from traces of chromium) and aquamarine. Also a main beryllium ore.

bonds.name: Beryllium copper
bonds.note: A spring and tool alloy (metal mix): strong, conducts, and won't spark when struck.

number.label: Stiffness (Young's modulus): about 40% above steel, at under a quarter of steel's weight

source: Mined mostly from the minerals bertrandite and beryl. These are turned into beryllium compounds. Then magnesium pulls the fluorine off beryllium fluoride, leaving the metal.

lenses.nexus: Copper-beryllium tools are common in refineries and petrochemical plants. There, a spark from a steel wrench could light hydrocarbon vapors.
lenses.rocket: Space telescopes like JWST and Spitzer used beryllium mirrors and frames. When every kilogram has to be launched, stiffness per kilogram is what counts.

name: Boron
tagline: The short-handed builder: after 3 handshakes it still has one empty hand, so it grabs electron pairs.
atomStory: Boron has 3 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring. It shares all 3 and holds hands with 3 partners. That only gets it to 6 of the 8 it wants, so one hand stays empty. That empty hand grabs electron pairs from other molecules. So boron compounds react easily and work as catalysts (helpers that speed up reactions).

uses.title: Borosilicate glass
uses.why: Boron oxide in the glass cuts how much it grows with heat to about a third of window glass. So lab glassware and oven dishes survive sudden heating and cooling.

uses.title: Armor and abrasives
uses.why: Boron carbide (B4C) is one of the hardest materials known, behind diamond and cubic boron nitride. Small boron and carbon atoms lock into a tight, rigid net of short bonds.

uses.title: Nuclear control rods
uses.why: The boron-10 nucleus (atom center) soaks up neutrons very well. So boron carbide rods, and boric acid in the coolant, slow a reactor down.

uses.title: Igniter fluid
uses.why: Triethylborane bursts into flame when it touches oxygen and burns with boron's green color. It is the TEB half of Falcon 9's TEA-TEB igniter.

uses.title: Neodymium magnets
uses.why: The strongest permanent magnets (Nd2Fe14B) need a little boron. It locks iron and neodymium into the crystal pattern that holds strong magnetism.

bonds.name: Triethylborane (TEB)
bonds.note: A liquid that catches fire on its own in air. Boron's empty hand gives oxygen an easy way in, so it ignites instantly.

bonds.name: Boron oxide
bonds.note: A glass maker: the boron ingredient in borosilicate glass and fiberglass.

bonds.name: Boron carbide
bonds.note: A very hard, light ceramic used in body armor, blasting nozzles and reactor control rods.

bonds.name: Boron nitride
bonds.note: Boron (3 outer electrons) plus nitrogen (5) has the same 8 as two carbons. So BN copies carbon: a slippery graphite-like form, and a diamond-like form nearly as hard as diamond.

number.label: Thermal expansion (growth when heated) of borosilicate glass: about a third of window glass

source: Mined as borate minerals like borax and kernite from old dried-up lake beds, mainly in Turkey and California.

lenses.nexus: Boron trifluoride (BF3) uses boron's empty hand to grab electron pairs. That makes it a strong acid catalyst for making polyisobutylene and other petrochemicals. It is a close cousin of the acid spots in zeolite catalysts.
lenses.rocket: Falcon 9's Merlin engines light with TEA-TEB, which ignites on touching liquid oxygen and flashes green from the boron. The Space Shuttle's black tiles had a borosilicate glass coating. It radiated heat away and sealed the porous silica underneath.

name: Carbon
tagline: The chain builder: four hands, and it happily holds hands with other carbons.
atomStory: Carbon has 4 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring, so it has 4 hands. It makes exactly 4 bonds. The atom is small, so carbon-to-carbon handshakes are short and strong. That lets carbon build long chains, rings and sheets. Because carbon holds hands with itself, there are millions of carbon compounds, from methane to polyethylene to living cells.

uses.title: Fuels
uses.why: Every hydrocarbon fuel stores energy in its C–C and C–H bonds. Burning trades them for stronger bonds in CO2 and H2O. The difference comes out as heat.

uses.title: Steel
uses.why: A fraction of a percent of carbon wedges between iron atoms. It keeps layers of atoms from sliding, turning soft iron into hard steel.

uses.title: Carbon fiber
uses.why: The fibers are graphite-like sheets lined up along their length. Carbon's strong bonds within each sheet give very high strength and stiffness per kg.

uses.title: Carbon-carbon heat shields
uses.why: Carbon doesn't melt at normal pressure. Above about 3,600 °C it turns straight to vapor. Reinforced carbon-carbon guarded the Shuttle's nose cap and wing leading (front) edges.

uses.title: Activated carbon
uses.why: Charcoal etched full of tiny pores can have over 1,000 m² of surface per gram. All that surface traps unwanted stuff from water and gas.

bonds.name: Diamond and graphite
bonds.note: Same atom, different handholds. Diamond uses all 4 hands in a 3D frame and is the hardest natural material. Graphite uses 3 in flat sheets with one loose electron, so it conducts and slides.

bonds.name: Methane
bonds.note: One carbon with each hand holding a hydrogen. Natural gas, Raptor's fuel, and the lightest pyrolysis gas.

bonds.name: Carbon oxides
bonds.note: CO2 is fully burned carbon, gripping each oxygen with two hands (two double bonds). CO is carbon short of oxygen. It is toxic, and a building block for making fuels.

bonds.name: Polyethylene
bonds.note: Thousands of carbons in a chain. Each uses 2 hands for its neighbors and 2 for hydrogens. The most common plastic.

number.label: Average energy to break a C–C vs a C–H bond: why chains crack before hydrogens strip off

source: Made in stars when three helium nuclei (atom centers) fuse. On Earth it cycles through air (CO2), living things, limestone and fossil fuels. Graphite and diamond are mined or made in factories.

lenses.nexus: At your plant, pyrolysis heat snaps the weaker C–C bonds in plastic chains first. That gives shorter pieces: gas, oil and wax. If hydrogen gets stripped off too, the leftover carbons bond to each other in sheets. That is char.
lenses.rocket: Starship burns methane (one carbon) instead of Falcon 9's RP-1 kerosene (about 12 carbons per molecule). Methane leaves far less coke (sooty buildup) in hot cooling channels. Starship's hull began as 304L stainless. The L means low carbon, so chromium carbides don't form at welds and invite rust. SpaceX has since moved to an in-house alloy reportedly called 30X.

name: Nitrogen
tagline: The locked-up gas: three hands, and in air it uses all three to grip one partner.
atomStory: Nitrogen has 5 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring and 3 hands. Two nitrogen atoms hold all 3 hands with each other. That triple bond is one of the strongest in chemistry. So the N2 that makes up 78% of air barely reacts. And any reaction that ends in N2 releases a lot of energy.

uses.title: Fertilizer
uses.why: The Haber-Bosch process forces N2 and H2 together over an iron catalyst (a helper that speeds the reaction). It runs near 450 °C and about 200 atmospheres. That breaks the triple bond and makes ammonia.

uses.title: Keeping oxygen out (purging)
uses.why: N2 barely reacts, so plants flood tanks, pipes and reactors with it. It pushes out oxygen and prevents fires.

uses.title: Liquid nitrogen
uses.why: It boils at -196 °C and is cheap because it comes straight from air. It is used to freeze food, cool equipment and run super-cold tests.

uses.title: Explosives
uses.why: TNT and ammonium nitrate hold nitrogen in weakly bonded forms. When the atoms snap together into N2, the triple bond's energy and the sudden burst of gas do the work.

bonds.name: Nitrogen gas
bonds.note: Two atoms in a three-handed grip (a triple bond). 78% of air and very hard to break apart.

bonds.name: Ammonia
bonds.note: Three hydrogens hold nitrogen's 3 hands. One unshared electron pair is left, which makes ammonia a base (the opposite of an acid). Nearly all fertilizer starts here.

bonds.name: Nitrogen tetroxide and hydrazine
bonds.note: A hypergolic pair: they ignite the moment they touch, no igniter needed. Hydrazine-family fuels power many spacecraft thrusters.

bonds.name: Nitrogen oxides (NOx)
bonds.note: Made when air's N2 and O2 meet in very hot flames. A smog source and a key emissions limit for furnaces and engines.

number.label: Energy to break the N≡N triple bond, about 2.7× a C–C bond

source: 78% of air by volume. Air is chilled until it turns liquid, then distilled (separated by boiling point). The same plants make liquid oxygen.

lenses.nexus: Pyrolysis reactors are flushed with nitrogen so the plastic cracks instead of burning. Plastics that contain nitrogen, like nylon and polyurethane, carry nitrogen compounds into the oil. Refiners don't want that contaminant.
lenses.rocket: Falcon 9 steers with nitrogen cold-gas thrusters (puffs of gas, no burning). Dragon's Draco thrusters burn nitrogen tetroxide with monomethylhydrazine. That hypergolic pair ignites the moment the two meet.

name: Oxygen
tagline: The electron grabber: two hands and a hard pull, so it reacts with almost everything and gives off energy doing it.
atomStory: Oxygen has 6 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring and 2 hands. Its 8 protons (+ particles) pull hard on a small ring. Only fluorine tugs shared electrons toward itself harder. When oxygen takes a fuel's electrons, the new bonds are stronger than the old ones. The difference comes out as heat.

uses.title: Rocket oxidizer
uses.why: Liquid oxygen is what methane, kerosene or hydrogen burn with. Raptor reportedly uses about 3.6 kg of oxygen per kg of methane. So close to 80% of Starship's propellant weight is oxygen.

uses.title: Steelmaking
uses.why: Blowing pure oxygen through molten iron burns extra carbon out as CO and CO2. That turns brittle pig iron into steel in well under an hour.

uses.title: Breathing and medicine
uses.why: When your cells burn food for energy, oxygen is the final electron grabber. That is why medical oxygen keeps patients alive when lungs struggle.

uses.title: Water treatment
uses.why: Ozone (O3) holds its third oxygen loosely and hands it off easily. That makes it a stronger oxidizer than O2. It kills germs without leaving chlorine behind.

bonds.name: Oxygen and ozone
bonds.note: In O2, two oxygens hold both hands (a double bond). O3 high in the stratosphere soaks up ultraviolet light before it reaches the ground.

bonds.name: Water
bonds.note: Oxygen's 2 hands each hold a hydrogen. Water is bent and its charge is lopsided, like a weak magnet. That gives water its unusual properties.

bonds.name: Carbon dioxide
bonds.note: Carbon grips each of two oxygens with two hands (double bonds). The end product of burning carbon, and the starting gas for the Sabatier reaction.

bonds.name: Silica
bonds.note: Each silicon holds 4 oxygens, and each oxygen bridges 2 silicons. That 3D net makes quartz, sand, glass and heat-shield tiles.

number.label: Density (weight for its size) of liquid oxygen, slightly more than water

source: 21% of air by volume, almost all put there by photosynthesis (plants using sunlight). Industry separates it from liquefied air. It is also the most common element in Earth's crust, about 46% by weight, locked in rock as oxides and silicates.

lenses.nexus: Oxygen is what pyrolysis at your plant keeps out. With air present, plastic burns to CO2 and water instead of cracking into oil. Plastics with oxygen in them, like PET, still bring it in. That leaves CO2, water and acids such as benzoic acid that can clog lines.
lenses.rocket: Liquid oxygen boils at -183 °C, so it is loaded close to launch and vents as white vapor. On Mars the plan is to make it there. The Sabatier reaction makes methane and water, and splitting that water gives oxygen.

name: Fluorine
tagline: The most aggressive atom: one hand and the strongest electron pull of any element.
atomStory: Fluorine has 7 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring and 1 hand. Its ring is small and close to 9 protons (+ particles). So it pulls on electrons harder than any other element and rips them from almost anything. But once it holds hands with carbon, it forms one of the strongest single bonds in chemistry. That is why Teflon barely reacts.

uses.title: Nonstick coatings and seals
uses.why: Teflon (PTFE) is a carbon chain fully wrapped in fluorine. The C–F bonds are so strong, and the fluorine coat so tight, that almost nothing sticks to it or attacks it.

uses.title: Toothpaste
uses.why: Fluoride swaps into tooth enamel to form fluorapatite. That stands up to acid better than the original mineral.

uses.title: Uranium enrichment
uses.why: UF6 turns to gas at about 56 °C. Fluorine has only one natural isotope (one atom weight). So weight differences between UF6 molecules come only from U-235 versus U-238. Centrifuges sort them by that tiny difference.

uses.title: Refrigerants
uses.why: Fluorinated hydrocarbons are stable gases that turn liquid easily under pressure. That makes them good working fluids for air conditioners and heat pumps.

bonds.name: Hydrogen fluoride
bonds.note: Hydrofluoric acid etches glass and soaks through skin to cause deep burns. It is the starting material for most fluorine chemicals.

bonds.name: PTFE (Teflon)
bonds.note: A polyethylene-like chain with fluorine in every spot a hydrogen would hold. Slippery, and it reacts with almost nothing.

bonds.name: Uranium hexafluoride
bonds.note: The only common uranium compound that turns to gas at a modest temperature. So it carries uranium through enrichment.

bonds.name: Fluorite
bonds.note: The main fluorine ore. Clear crystals also make lenses that pass ultraviolet and infrared light.

number.label: Electronegativity (how hard it pulls electrons, Pauling scale), the highest of any element

source: Mined as fluorite (CaF2) and reacted with sulfuric acid to make HF. Pure fluorine gas is made by electrolysis (splitting with electricity), first done by Henri Moissan in 1886.

lenses.nexus: Many refineries use liquid HF as the acid catalyst (reaction helper) in alkylation units. These join isobutane to propylene and butylenes to make high-octane gasoline blendstock.
lenses.rocket: Liquid fluorine was tested as an oxidizer (what fuel burns with) because it beats oxygen. But it is so toxic and corrosive, and its exhaust so full of HF, that no operational launch vehicle ever used it.

name: Neon
tagline: The sealed ring: its outer ring is full at 8, so it has no hands. It bonds with nothing and only glows.
atomStory: Neon's outer ring is full, so it has no hands: nothing to share and no room to take. Its electrons (tiny − particles) are held very tightly. Neon has no known stable compounds. Run electricity through it and its electrons jump to higher rings. Then they drop back and give off red-orange light at wavelengths (exact shades) unique to neon.

uses.title: Neon signs
uses.why: Excited neon electrons fall back to their normal rings and give off red-orange light. Other sign colors come from other gases or from coatings on the tube.

uses.title: Chip-making lasers
uses.why: Neon is the main filler gas in the excimer lasers used to print computer chips. It carries energy around the laser without reacting.

uses.title: Helium-neon lasers
uses.why: Helium passes energy to neon atoms. Neon then gives off steady red light at 632.8 nm for alignment and measuring tools.

uses.title: Cryogenic cooling
uses.why: Liquid neon boils at -246 °C. It fills the gap between liquid nitrogen and liquid helium for some cooling jobs.

number.label: Energy to pull off one electron, second only to helium

source: Only about 18 parts per million of air. It is collected as a side product of the big air-separation plants that make oxygen and nitrogen.

name: Sodium
tagline: The give-away metal: one lonely outer electron that it hands to almost anything.
atomStory: Sodium has full inner rings of 2 and 8. Then one electron (tiny − particle) sits alone on a third ring, far from the center. It is easy to lose, so sodium gives it away and becomes Na+. That leaves a full ring underneath. The metal is soft enough to cut with a knife. It reacts with water hard enough to light the hydrogen it releases.

uses.title: Salt and chemicals
uses.why: Rock salt and seawater (NaCl) feed the chemical industry. Running electricity through salt water splits it into chlorine and caustic soda (NaOH).

uses.title: Street lamps
uses.why: Sodium vapor lamps glow yellow at 589 nm as excited electrons drop back down. They are very efficient but show colors poorly.

uses.title: Laser guide stars
uses.why: Meteors leave a thin layer of sodium atoms about 90 km up, in the mesosphere. Observatories shine a 589 nm laser on it to make a fake star. That helps them correct blur from the air.

uses.title: Heat-transfer coolant
uses.why: Liquid sodium melts at 98 °C and stays liquid to 883 °C. Its loose electrons carry heat well. It cools some fast nuclear reactors and the hollow exhaust valves in some high-performance engines.

bonds.name: Sodium chloride
bonds.note: Sodium hands its electron to chlorine. Now one is + and one is −, and they stick like magnets. They stack into cube-shaped crystals: table salt.

bonds.name: Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda)
bonds.note: A strong base (the opposite of an acid). Used to make soap, pull alumina out of bauxite, and neutralize acids.

bonds.name: Sodium carbonate (soda ash)
bonds.note: The main flux in ordinary glass: it lowers the heat needed to melt sand.

number.label: Melting point, below the boiling point of water

source: Made by running electricity through melted sodium chloride. Sodium metal forms at one end and chlorine gas at the other.

lenses.nexus: Refineries and pyrolysis plants use caustic soda washes to neutralize acids and scrub out hydrogen sulfide. One such acid is HCl, which comes from PVC in the plastic feed.

name: Magnesium
tagline: The light structural metal: two loose electrons to give away, and two-thirds the weight of aluminum.
atomStory: Magnesium has 2 loosely held electrons (tiny − particles) on its third ring. It gives both away and becomes Mg2+. Joining with oxygen releases so much energy that magnesium burns with a blinding white flame. It keeps burning even in CO2. As a solid, it is the lightest metal used for structures.

uses.title: Lightweight castings
uses.why: Car parts, laptop and camera bodies, and aircraft gearbox housings use magnesium alloys (metal mixes). They weigh less than aluminum ones.

uses.title: Aluminum alloys
uses.why: A few percent magnesium in aluminum, often with silicon as in 6061, forms tiny specks. These stop layers of atoms from slipping, making the alloy much stronger.

uses.title: Titanium production
uses.why: The Kroll process uses molten magnesium to pull chlorine off TiCl4, leaving titanium metal. It works because magnesium holds chlorine tighter than titanium does.

uses.title: Flares and fireworks
uses.why: Burning magnesium gives off so much heat that the MgO it forms glows brilliant white.

uses.title: Furnace linings
uses.why: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2,850 °C. So MgO bricks line steel furnaces and cement kilns.

bonds.name: Magnesium oxide
bonds.note: Mg2+ and O2- grip each other very tightly, like strong magnets. The result is a heat-proof ceramic that melts near 2,850 °C.

bonds.name: Magnesium chloride
bonds.note: Found in seawater and brines. Also the base that holds titanium in modern plastic-making catalysts.

bonds.name: Chlorophyll a
bonds.note: A single magnesium ion sits at the center of the molecule plants use to catch sunlight.

number.label: Density (weight for its size), about two-thirds of aluminum: the lightest structural metal

source: Made mostly by the Pidgeon process: roasted dolomite is heated with ferrosilicon to drive off magnesium vapor. It is also made by running electricity through magnesium chloride from seawater or brine.

lenses.nexus: Most polypropylene and much polyethylene are made on Ziegler-Natta catalysts (helpers that link the chains). These are titanium chloride spread on magnesium chloride, switched on by triethylaluminum. Much of the plastic arriving at your plant was built on magnesium.

name: Aluminum
tagline: The light, self-sealing metal: it gives away three electrons but hides under an oxide skin a few nanometers thick.
atomStory: Aluminum has 3 electrons (tiny − particles) on its third ring. It gives them away to become Al3+. It reacts with oxygen instantly. But the oxide skin is tight and only a few nanometers thick. It seals the metal underneath instead of flaking off like rust. In the solid metal, each atom's 3 pooled electrons make aluminum a good conductor.

uses.title: Aircraft and rocket structures
uses.why: Aluminum is about a third as dense as steel, and strong once alloyed (mixed with other metals). Falcon 9's propellant tanks are an aluminum-lithium alloy.

uses.title: Power lines
uses.why: Aluminum conducts about 61% as well as the same volume of copper but weighs about a third as much. So it carries more current per kg and rules overhead lines.

uses.title: Solid rocket propellant
uses.why: Fine aluminum powder burns to Al2O3 and gives off a lot of heat. The Space Shuttle boosters' propellant was about 16% aluminum, mixed with ammonium perchlorate oxidizer.

uses.title: Cans and foil
uses.why: Aluminum rolls thinner than paper and blocks light, air and moisture. Recycling it takes only about 5% of the energy of making new metal.

bonds.name: Alumina
bonds.note: The protective skin on the metal. Also the hard mineral corundum (ruby and sapphire), a common catalyst support, and the white smoke from solid rocket boosters.

bonds.name: Triethylaluminum (TEA)
bonds.note: A liquid that catches fire on contact with air. The TEA in Falcon 9's TEA-TEB igniter, and the activator in Ziegler-Natta catalysts.

bonds.name: Aluminosilicates (zeolites, clays)
bonds.note: When Al3+ takes a Si4+ spot in a silica frame, the frame ends up one + charge short. An H+ fills the gap and becomes a strong acid spot for cracking.

number.label: Density (weight for its size), about a third of steel

source: The most common metal in Earth's crust, refined from bauxite ore. First the Bayer process dissolves out alumina with caustic soda. Then Hall-Héroult cells split melted alumina with electricity at about 960 °C. That takes roughly 13 to 15 kWh per kg of metal.

lenses.nexus: Zeolite and clay cracking catalysts (helpers that speed up chain-breaking) get their acid spots from aluminum atoms in a silica frame. More aluminum means more acid spots. Triethylaluminum also activates the catalysts that make polyethylene and polypropylene.
lenses.rocket: Aluminum alloys lose much of their strength at a few hundred °C and melt at 660 °C. Stainless steel melts at about 1,400 °C. That is one reason Starship went with steel. Falcon 9 keeps aluminum-lithium tanks, and solid boosters burn aluminum powder.

name: Silicon
tagline: Carbon's bigger cousin: four hands like carbon, but it prefers oxygen, so it builds rock and glass instead of chains.
atomStory: Silicon has 4 electrons (tiny − particles) on its outer ring, so like carbon it has 4 hands. But that ring sits one ring farther out. So Si–Si handshakes are long and weak, while Si–O ones are about twice as strong. That is why Earth's silicon is locked in sand, quartz and clay, not long chains.

uses.title: Computer chips
uses.why: In a pure crystal, every silicon holds all 4 hands with neighbors, so few electrons are free. A trace of boron (3 outer electrons) leaves holes. Phosphorus (5) adds spare electrons. That lets engineers control exactly where current flows.

uses.title: Solar cells
uses.why: Silicon's band gap, about 1.1 eV, is the energy kick needed to free an electron. It suits sunlight: visible and near-infrared photons (light particles) carry enough to knock electrons loose and make current.

uses.title: Heat-shield tiles
uses.why: Space Shuttle tiles were over 90% empty space inside a mat of pure silica fibers. Silica moves heat poorly and barely grows when hot. A tile could be held by its edges seconds after leaving a 1,260 °C oven.

uses.title: Silicones
uses.why: A backbone of silicon and oxygen taking turns, with methyl groups attached. The strong Si–O chain makes sealants and rubbers that stay bendy across a wide range, roughly -50 to 200 °C and beyond.

bonds.name: Silica
bonds.note: Every silicon holds 4 oxygens in a 3D net: quartz, sand, glass, and the fibers in heat-shield tiles.

bonds.name: Silicon carbide
bonds.note: Silicon and carbon both have 4 hands, so they form a diamond-like frame. Very hard and heat resistant. Used in abrasives (grinding grit), brake discs and power electronics.

bonds.name: Silicone (PDMS)
bonds.note: The most common silicone. The Shuttle glued its tiles to the airframe with a silicone adhesive.

bonds.name: Zeolites and clays
bonds.note: Silica frames with some silicon swapped for aluminum. Their pores and acid spots make them cracking catalysts (helpers that speed up chain-breaking).

number.label: Thermal expansion (growth when heated) of fused silica, about 1/30 of stainless steel: the root of the tile-joint mismatch

source: About 28% of Earth's crust by weight, second only to oxygen. Quartz is heated with carbon in electric arc furnaces near 2,000 °C (SiO2 + 2C → Si + 2CO). For chips it is then purified to better than 99.9999999%.

lenses.nexus: Zeolite and clay catalysts are silicon-oxygen frames with pores that work like a sieve, letting only certain molecules in. Aluminum spots in the frame do the cracking. Together they steer which product sizes come out of the reactor.
lenses.rocket: Starship's roughly 18,000 heat-shield tiles are reported to be silica-based, like the Shuttle's. Silica insulates and survives sudden temperature swings. The weak point is the joint. The steel hull grows about 30 times as much per degree as silica, so the attachment has to absorb the difference.

name: Phosphorus
tagline: The life and fertilizer element: 5 outer electrons and 3 hands to hold out.
atomStory: Phosphorus has 5 electrons (tiny charged bits) in its outer layer and 3 hands. So in simple molecules like PH3 it holds 3 hands, just like nitrogen above it. Its atom is bigger than nitrogen's, so it can fit more partners around itself. That gives phosphate (PO4 3-), the form life and industry use most.

uses.title: Fertilizer
uses.why: Plants need phosphate to build DNA and ATP. ATP is the molecule cells use to move energy around. Nothing can replace it, so most mined phosphate rock goes to farms.

uses.title: DNA and ATP
uses.why: Phosphate groups link DNA's sugars into a backbone, like the rails of a ladder. ATP has three phosphates in a row. Snapping one off releases stored energy.

uses.title: Tuning silicon for chips
uses.why: Phosphorus has 5 outer electrons; silicon has 4. Swap a few phosphorus atoms into a silicon crystal. Each one brings a spare electron that is free to carry current. This is n-type silicon, used in solar cells and chips.

uses.title: Match strikers
uses.why: The strip on a matchbox holds red phosphorus. Rubbing turns a tiny bit of it into the more reactive white form. That lights the match head.

bonds.name: Phosphate
bonds.note: One phosphorus with four oxygens around it. The form found in rock, bone, fertilizer and DNA.

bonds.name: Phosphoric acid
bonds.note: Made from phosphate rock and sulfuric acid. The starting point for fertilizers, and the tang in cola.

bonds.name: Phosphorus pentoxide
bonds.note: What phosphorus becomes when it burns. It pulls in water so hard that it is used to dry things.

bonds.name: Phosphine
bonds.note: Phosphorus with 3 hydrogens holding its 3 hands. A toxic gas used to gas out pests (fumigation) and in chip making.

number.label: Year Hennig Brand got it out of boiled-down urine. The first element found by a person we know by name

source: Mined as phosphate rock from ancient seabeds. The main mineral is apatite, a calcium phosphate. Morocco holds most known reserves.

lenses.nexus: Phosphorus flame retardants in plastics turn into a protective char crust when heated. Solid phosphoric acid catalysts (helpers that speed a reaction without being used up) join propylene and butylene into gasoline-size molecules. Phosphorus also keeps ZSM-5 zeolite catalyst stable in refinery FCC units.

name: Sulfur
tagline: Oxygen's bigger cousin with 2 hands: the backbone of sulfuric acid and tire rubber.
atomStory: Sulfur sits right under oxygen. It has 6 outer electrons and 2 hands, so it holds 2 hands. That is why H2S looks just like H2O. Sulfur's atom is bigger and holds its electrons more loosely. So it can also hold up to four oxygens (sulfate), and hold hands with itself in chains and rings.

uses.title: Sulfuric acid
uses.why: Burn sulfur to get SO2, then SO3, then add water. That gives H2SO4, the most-made industrial chemical by weight. This strong acid dissolves phosphate rock for fertilizer and pulls metals out of ore.

uses.title: Curing tire rubber (vulcanizing)
uses.why: With 2 hands, sulfur can act as a bridge. It ties one long rubber molecule (a polymer chain) to the next. Those links make tires spring back instead of slowly flowing like putty.

uses.title: Fertilizer
uses.why: Plants need sulfur to build two amino acids (cysteine and methionine), which are protein building blocks. So sulfate is added to many fertilizers.

uses.title: Gunpowder
uses.why: Black powder is about 10% sulfur. It lowers the temperature at which the charcoal and potassium nitrate mix catches fire.

bonds.name: Hydrogen sulfide
bonds.note: The rotten-egg gas in sour natural gas and crude oil. It is toxic and eats metal, so refineries strip it out.

bonds.name: Sulfur dioxide
bonds.note: What sulfur in fuel turns into when burned. It causes acid rain, which is why fuel has sulfur limits.

bonds.name: Sulfuric acid
bonds.note: Sulfur holding four oxygens. The workhorse acid of industry.

bonds.name: Pyrite
bonds.note: Fool's gold: shiny brass-colored crystals of iron and sulfur, common in coal and rock.

number.label: Atoms in each crown-shaped ring of solid yellow sulfur (S8)

source: Most sulfur today comes out of sour natural gas and crude oil. The Claus process turns their H2S into solid sulfur. Some is still mined from underground.

lenses.nexus: Crude oil carries sulfur. Refineries pull it out with hydrogen (hydrodesulfurization) and collect it as pure sulfur. Polyethylene and polypropylene have almost none, so oil made from plastic starts low in sulfur. But tire rubber feed brings its curing sulfur along.

name: Chlorine
tagline: Just 1 empty hand, and it grabs electrons hard: salt, PVC, bleach.
atomStory: Chlorine has 7 outer electrons and just 1 hand. Its center (nucleus) pulls hard to fill it. Next to a metal, it simply takes an electron and becomes Cl- (as in table salt). With carbon or hydrogen it shares instead, holding exactly 1 hand.

uses.title: PVC plastic
uses.why: PVC is a chain like polyethylene, but with a chlorine on every other carbon. It is about 57% chlorine by weight. The carbon-chlorine bonds make it stiff and slow to burn, because loose chlorine disrupts the flame's chemistry.

uses.title: Cleaning drinking water
uses.why: In water, chlorine forms hypochlorous acid (HOCl). It rips electrons off the molecules of bacteria and viruses, which kills them.

uses.title: Bleach
uses.why: Household bleach is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl). The same electron-stealing breaks down colored molecules and germs.

uses.title: Hydrochloric acid
uses.why: HCl in water is a strong acid. It cleans rust and scale off steel before coating (called pickling). Your stomach uses it too.

bonds.name: Sodium chloride
bonds.note: Table salt. Sodium gives its 1 loose electron to chlorine's 1 empty hand. Now one is + and one is −, and they stick like magnets into a crystal.

bonds.name: Hydrogen chloride
bonds.note: A gas that becomes hydrochloric acid in water. Also what PVC gives off when heated.

bonds.name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
bonds.note: Plastic for pipe, siding and wire coating. The plastic in mixed waste that carries chlorine.

bonds.name: Sodium hypochlorite
bonds.note: The active ingredient in liquid bleach.

number.label: Energy released when a chlorine atom grabs an electron. No element releases more (highest electron affinity)

source: Made by running electricity through salty water (the chlor-alkali process). That splits it into chlorine gas, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

lenses.nexus: PVC is the problem plastic for pyrolysis. From about 250-300 °C it gives off HCl. That eats away steel and leaves chlorine in the oil. So plants limit PVC in the feed and often remove chlorine from the product.
lenses.rocket: Ammonium perchlorate (NH4ClO4) is the oxidizer, the oxygen supplier, in most solid rocket boosters. It was about 70% of the Space Shuttle booster propellant by weight. Each chlorine carries four oxygens. It hands them over to burn the aluminum and rubbery binder.

name: Argon
tagline: The lazy gas: no empty hands, so it reacts with almost nothing.
atomStory: Argon has 8 electrons in its outer layer, and that layer is full. It has 0 hands to hold out. It gains nothing by sharing, giving or taking electrons. So it forms almost no stable compounds. Its name comes from the Greek word for idle.

uses.title: Welding shield gas
uses.why: A stream of argon covers the melted metal like a blanket. Oxygen and nitrogen from the air can't reach it and weaken the weld. It works because argon won't react even at welding heat.

uses.title: Making stainless steel
uses.why: In argon-oxygen decarburization, argon is blown in with oxygen to thin it out. Carbon burns out of the melted steel, while the valuable chromium stays put.

uses.title: Light bulbs
uses.why: Old-style bulbs were filled with argon so the hot tungsten wire couldn't react with oxygen. The gas also slowed the wire from boiling away.

uses.title: Insulated windows
uses.why: Argon is heavier than air and carries heat less well. Filling the gap in double-pane windows cuts heat loss.

number.label: Share of Earth's air. The third most common gas, after nitrogen and oxygen

source: Separated by distilling liquid air. Almost all of Earth's argon is argon-40. It was made over billions of years as radioactive potassium-40 broke down in rocks.

lenses.rocket: SpaceX's Starlink V2 Mini satellites use Hall-effect thrusters that run on argon (company-reported). They push out charged argon atoms (ions). Those are heavy enough for useful thrust, and argon costs far less than xenon, the usual electric-thruster fuel.

name: Potassium
tagline: One lonely outer electron, far from the center: potash, nerves, and gunpowder.
atomStory: Potassium has a single electron alone in its 4th layer. It sits far from the center, behind 18 other electrons. Potassium gives it away with almost no effort and becomes K+. That makes it even more reactive than sodium above it.

uses.title: Fertilizer (potash)
uses.why: Plants use K+ to open and close tiny pores in their leaves and to move water. Potassium is one of the three main fertilizer nutrients (N-P-K).

uses.title: Nerve and muscle signals
uses.why: Your cells pump K+ in and Na+ out. When these charged atoms (ions) rush back across the cell's outer skin, that is the electric pulse behind every nerve signal and heartbeat.

uses.title: Gunpowder oxidizer
uses.why: Potassium nitrate (KNO3) is about 75% of black powder. It carries oxygen and lets it go when heated, so the powder burns without air.

uses.title: Alkaline battery fluid
uses.why: Potassium hydroxide splits into K+ and OH- ions that move freely. They carry charge between the zinc and manganese dioxide inside an AA battery.

bonds.name: Potassium chloride
bonds.note: The main potash mineral (sylvite) and a salt substitute. K gives its one electron to Cl's one empty hand.

bonds.name: Potassium nitrate
bonds.note: Saltpeter: the oxygen source in gunpowder, and a fertilizer.

bonds.name: Potassium hydroxide
bonds.note: A strong base (the opposite of an acid) used in soaps, battery fluid and making biodiesel.

bonds.name: Potassium carbonate
bonds.note: First made by soaking wood ash and boiling it in pots. That gave potash, and potassium, their names.

number.label: Time for half of potassium-40 to break down (its half-life). It is the radioactive kind in every banana, and it made most of Earth's argon

source: Mined as potash: beds of potassium chloride left behind when ancient seas dried up. The pure metal is made by reacting melted KCl with sodium.

lenses.nexus: Potassium boosts the iron oxide catalyst (a reaction helper) that turns ethylbenzene into styrene. It helps steam burn off coke, a carbon crust, so the catalyst keeps working longer.
lenses.rocket: The first rockets, Chinese fire arrows and British Congreve rockets, ran on black powder. Potassium nitrate was the oxidizer, the part that supplies oxygen. Same fuel-plus-oxidizer idea as a modern rocket.

name: Calcium
tagline: Gives away 2 outer electrons, and builds bone, limestone and cement.
atomStory: Calcium has 2 electrons in its outer layer and gives both away. That makes it Ca2+, a double plus charge. It grips negative pieces like carbonate and phosphate tightly, like a strong magnet. That is why calcium compounds are hard, stable solids: shells, bone, limestone and concrete.

uses.title: Cement and concrete
uses.why: Heating limestone drives off CO2 and leaves lime (CaO). In cement, calcium silicates react with water. They grow crystals that lock together and harden into rock.

uses.title: Bones and teeth
uses.why: Bone mineral is hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate. The tight grip between Ca2+ and phosphate makes it hard.

uses.title: Cleaning steel (flux)
uses.why: Lime added to a steel furnace grabs silica, phosphorus and sulfur. They form a floating layer called slag, which is skimmed off.

uses.title: Drywall and plaster
uses.why: Gypsum is calcium sulfate with water locked inside. Heat drives off some water. Add water back and it sets hard again.

bonds.name: Calcium carbonate
bonds.note: Limestone, chalk, marble and seashells. Mostly built by sea life over millions of years.

bonds.name: Calcium oxide (lime)
bonds.note: Made by roasting limestone near 900 °C. The base of cement, and used to clean steel.

bonds.name: Hydroxyapatite
bonds.note: The mineral in bone and tooth enamel.

bonds.name: Gypsum
bonds.note: The mineral inside drywall and plaster.

number.label: Share of the body's calcium that sits in bones and teeth

source: Mined as limestone and chalk, rock made mostly from the shells of ancient sea creatures. The fifth most common element in Earth's crust.

lenses.nexus: Calcium carbonate is a cheap filler in many plastics. In pyrolysis it ends up as ash in the char. Lime can also be added to catch HCl from PVC. It locks the chlorine up as calcium chloride before it reaches the oil.

name: Scandium
tagline: The first transition metal (middle-block metal): a pinch of it makes aluminum stronger.
atomStory: Scandium is where electrons start filling an inner layer (the 3d shell) instead of the outer one. It has 3 electrons it can give: 2 outer and 1 in 3d. It nearly always gives all three and becomes Sc3+. From here on the inner d electrons join in, so simple hand-counting stops working.

uses.title: Aluminum-scandium alloys
uses.why: An alloy is a metal mix. A few tenths of a percent of scandium forms tiny Al3Sc specks that pin aluminum's crystal grains in place. The metal gets stronger and keeps more strength after welding. Used in some aerospace parts and high-end bike frames.

uses.title: Stadium and film lights
uses.why: Scandium iodide in metal halide lamps gives off many sharp colors of light at once. Together they make bright light close to daylight.

uses.title: Solid oxide fuel cells
uses.why: Adding scandium oxide to zirconia leaves gaps in the crystal. Charged oxygen atoms (ions) hop through those gaps. That is how these fuel cells carry current.

bonds.name: Scandium oxide
bonds.note: The form scandium is sold in. Used in fuel cells and to make the metal.

bonds.name: Scandium iodide
bonds.note: The salt that gives off the light in metal halide lamps.

bonds.name: Aluminum scandide
bonds.note: Super tiny (nanoscale) specks inside Al-Sc alloys that stop crystal grains from growing.

number.label: Density (weight for its size), barely heavier than aluminum (2.70 g/cm³)

source: Spread thin through many minerals, with almost no rich ores. So it is collected as a side product when processing titanium, uranium, rare earth and nickel ores.

name: Titanium
tagline: Strong like steel at about half the weight, sealed by its own oxide skin.
atomStory: Titanium has 4 electrons it can give: 2 outer and 2 in the inner 3d layer. It usually gives all four, as in TiO2. It grabs oxygen so fast that any bare surface instantly grows an oxide skin (metal joined with oxygen). The skin is only a few nanometers thick, far thinner than a hair. It seals the metal, which is why titanium shrugs off corrosion.

uses.title: Aircraft and spacecraft
uses.why: Titanium alloys (metal mixes) match many steels in strength at about 57% of the weight. They stay strong at heat that softens aluminum. So they go into airframes, landing gear, and jet engine fans and compressors.

uses.title: Medical implants
uses.why: The oxide skin is stable and the body accepts it. Bone even grows onto it. So hip joints and dental implants are made of titanium.

uses.title: White pigment
uses.why: Titanium dioxide bends light very strongly. A thin layer scatters nearly all visible light, so it looks bright white. Most mined titanium ends up as this pigment in paint, plastic and paper.

uses.title: Seawater and chemical equipment
uses.why: The self-repairing skin resists salt water and chlorine. So titanium is used for desalination tubes and chemical plant heat exchangers.

bonds.name: Titanium dioxide
bonds.note: The mineral rutile, and the world's main white pigment.

bonds.name: Titanium tetrachloride
bonds.note: A liquid made on the way to titanium metal. Also the active part of Ziegler-Natta catalysts that make plastic.

bonds.name: Grade 5 titanium alloy
bonds.note: About 90% titanium, 6% aluminum, 4% vanadium. The most-used titanium alloy in aerospace.

number.label: Density (weight for its size), about 57% of steel's (7.9 g/cm³)

source: Mined from beach sands rich in ilmenite (FeTiO3) and rutile (TiO2). The Kroll process turns ore into TiCl4, then melted magnesium strips off the chlorine. It is slow and done one batch at a time, which is why titanium is expensive.

lenses.nexus: Most polypropylene and much of the world's polyethylene is made on Ziegler-Natta catalysts (reaction helpers). They are titanium chloride on a magnesium chloride base, switched on by triethylaluminum. That is the same TEA as in Falcon 9's TEA-TEB igniter. Small building blocks (monomers) snap onto the titanium one at a time to grow the chain.
lenses.rocket: Falcon 9's grid fins are titanium. SpaceX switched from aluminum fins, which could catch fire during reentry. Titanium alloys also show up in rocket and spacecraft frames and pressure tanks, where weight and heat both matter.

name: Vanadium
tagline: A metal with four colorful charges: tough steel, a sulfuric acid helper, flow batteries.
atomStory: Vanadium has 5 electrons it can give: 2 outer and 3 in the inner 3d layer. It can give up 2, 3, 4 or all 5. In water, each of those charges shows a different color: violet, green, blue, yellow. The inner d electrons join in here, so hand-counting doesn't work.

uses.title: Tough steel
uses.why: A few tenths of a percent of vanadium forms hard vanadium carbide specks. They keep steel's crystal grains small. That makes tool steel, springs and rebar stronger and tougher.

uses.title: Flow batteries
uses.why: These batteries store energy by shifting vanadium between charges in two tanks of liquid. Both sides use the same element. So if liquid leaks across the divider, it doesn't ruin the battery fluid.

uses.title: Sulfuric acid catalyst
uses.why: A catalyst is a helper that is never used up. Vanadium pentoxide hands an oxygen to SO2 to make SO3, dropping from +5 to +4. Then it grabs oxygen from the air and goes back.

uses.title: Titanium alloy
uses.why: Vanadium is the 4 in Ti-6Al-4V. It holds titanium in a second crystal form, which lets the alloy be heat-treated for strength.

bonds.name: Vanadium pentoxide
bonds.note: Orange helper (catalyst) for making sulfuric acid. Vanadium at its full +5.

bonds.name: Vanadium carbide
bonds.note: Very hard specks that strengthen steel.

bonds.name: Vanadyl sulfate
bonds.note: Blue salt used to make flow battery fluid.

number.label: Charges vanadium takes in water (+2 to +5), each a different color. The basis of the vanadium flow battery

source: Mostly a side product of steelmaking slag (furnace waste) from iron ore that holds vanadium. Some also comes from oil residues and ash.

lenses.nexus: Heavy crude carries vanadium locked inside ring-shaped carbon molecules. In a refinery FCC unit it lands on the zeolite catalyst and wrecks its structure. So vanadium is a key catalyst poison. Oils made from plastic are mostly free of it.

name: Chromium
tagline: The element that makes stainless steel stainless.
atomStory: Chromium moves one outer electron inward, so its 3d layer is exactly half full (5 of 10). That setup is more stable, and it leaves one electron outside. Chromium grabs oxygen fast. It forms an oxide skin only a few nanometers thick. The skin is tight and repairs itself when scratched.

uses.title: Stainless steel
uses.why: Steel with at least about 10.5% chromium grows an unbroken chromium oxide film that blocks rust. Scratch it, and the exposed chromium reseals with oxygen.

uses.title: Chrome plating
uses.why: A thin chromium layer is put on with electricity (electroplating). It is hard and stays shiny because of the same oxide film.

uses.title: Gem and pigment colors
uses.why: A trace of Cr3+ in aluminum oxide makes ruby red. In beryl it makes emerald green. Chromium's d electrons soak up certain colors of light.

uses.title: Leather tanning
uses.why: Chromium(III) salts link the collagen fibers in animal hide together, turning it into tough leather. Most leather is chrome-tanned.

bonds.name: Chromium(III) oxide
bonds.note: The protective film on stainless steel, and a stable green pigment.

bonds.name: Chromate and dichromate (hexavalent chromium)
bonds.note: Chromium at +6. Strong electron-stealers (oxidizers) known to cause cancer, so they are tightly regulated.

bonds.name: Chromite
bonds.note: The only chromium ore mined for business.

number.label: Least chromium steel can have and still count as stainless

source: Mined as chromite ore. It is smelted with carbon into ferrochrome, an iron-chromium mix that goes straight into steelmaking.

lenses.nexus: Chromium on silica (the Phillips catalyst, a reaction helper) makes a large share of the world's high-density polyethylene. Chromia on alumina turns propane into propylene by pulling hydrogen off its C-H bonds.
lenses.rocket: Starship's hull and tanks are stainless steel. Early ships used 304L, about 18% chromium and 8% nickel. SpaceX has since moved to its own alloy, reportedly called 30X. Stainless stays strong at liquid-oxygen cold and melts around 1,400 °C, versus aluminum's 660 °C. So only the side facing the oncoming air needs heat-shield tiles.

name: Manganese
tagline: Steel's cleanup crew, with charges from +2 up to purple +7.
atomStory: Manganese has 7 electrons it can give: 2 outer and 5 in a half-full 3d layer. It can give anywhere from 2 (Mn2+) up to all 7, as in purple permanganate (MnO4-). The inner d electrons join in, so hand-counting breaks down.

uses.title: Steelmaking
uses.why: Most manganese goes into steel. It grabs leftover oxygen and sulfur. It forms manganese sulfide instead of iron sulfide, which would make steel crack when rolled hot.

uses.title: Alkaline batteries
uses.why: Manganese dioxide is the + end (cathode) in AA batteries. It takes in electrons by stepping down from Mn4+ to Mn3+.

uses.title: Aluminum cans
uses.why: About 1% manganese makes the aluminum in drink cans stronger, without making it harder to shape.

uses.title: Water treatment
uses.why: Potassium permanganate is a strong electron-stealer (oxidizer). It pulls electrons from iron, sulfide and carbon-based gunk so they can be filtered out.

bonds.name: Manganese dioxide
bonds.note: The main ore mineral (pyrolusite) and a battery cathode material.

bonds.name: Potassium permanganate
bonds.note: Deep purple electron-stealer, with manganese at +7.

bonds.name: Manganese sulfide
bonds.note: Harmless specks that lock up sulfur in steel.

number.label: Highest charge, reached in permanganate by giving up all seven 3d and 4s electrons

source: Mined mostly as manganese oxide ores. Potato-sized lumps on the deep seafloor hold large amounts, but they are not mined for business yet.

lenses.rocket: The V-2 spun its turbopump with steam made from hydrogen peroxide. A permanganate solution broke the peroxide down, acting as a catalyst (a helper that is not used up). This peroxide turbine idea carried into early postwar rockets.

name: Iron
tagline: Steel, blood and magnets: the metal where stars' fusion chain ends.
atomStory: Iron usually gives up 2 or 3 electrons (Fe2+ or Fe3+), from both its outer layer and its 3d layer. Four of its 3d electrons are unpaired. In the metal, their spins line up across neighbor atoms like tiny compass needles. That makes iron magnetic. Its center (nucleus) is among the most tightly held together of all.

uses.title: Steel
uses.why: Steel is iron with about 0.1-1% carbon. The small carbon atoms wedge into gaps in iron's crystal. They stop layers from sliding, which turns soft iron into strong steel.

uses.title: Stainless steel hulls
uses.why: Stainless is still about 70% iron, with chromium to stop rust and nickel for toughness.

uses.title: Blood
uses.why: Each hemoglobin molecule holds four Fe2+ atoms. They hold oxygen loosely enough to let it go in your muscles.

uses.title: Magnets and transformer cores
uses.why: Unpaired 3d electrons line up their spins. So iron gathers magnetic fields in motors and transformers.

uses.title: Ammonia catalyst
uses.why: The Haber-Bosch process uses iron as a helper (catalyst). It splits nitrogen's triple bond, three hands held at once, so nitrogen can join hydrogen. That makes ammonia for fertilizer.

bonds.name: Iron(III) oxide
bonds.note: Rust and the ore hematite. Also the red in Mars's dust.

bonds.name: Magnetite
bonds.note: Black magnetic iron ore that holds both Fe2+ and Fe3+.

bonds.name: Cementite
bonds.note: Hard iron-carbon compound that forms in carbon steel and cast iron.

number.label: How tightly each particle in iron-56's center is held (binding energy), near the top. Stars that fuse heavier atoms spend energy instead of making it

source: Mined as hematite and magnetite ores. A blast furnace burns coke (baked coal) into carbon monoxide, which pulls the oxygen off the ore. Newer plants use natural gas or hydrogen instead.

lenses.nexus: Iron catalysts (reaction helpers) drive Fischer-Tropsch synthesis. It builds chains of carbon and hydrogen from CO and H2. That is pyrolysis in reverse: your plant breaks long chains apart, and this builds them up.
lenses.rocket: Starship is built from stainless steel, about 70% iron. SpaceX switched from carbon fiber around the turn of 2019. Steel is cheap and easy to weld. It stays strong from -183 °C liquid oxygen up to heat that would soften aluminum.

name: Cobalt
tagline: The deep-blue magnetic metal inside many lithium-ion batteries.
atomStory: Cobalt usually gives up 2 or 3 electrons, from both its outer layer and its 3d layer. Like iron and nickel, it has unpaired 3d electrons whose spins line up, so it is magnetic. It stays magnetic at a higher temperature than any other element.

uses.title: Lithium-ion batteries
uses.why: In lithium cobalt oxide cathodes (the battery's + end), cobalt shifts between +3 and +4 as lithium ions leave and come back. Meanwhile it holds the layered crystal steady.

uses.title: Superalloys and hard coatings
uses.why: Cobalt alloys (metal mixes) stay strong and hard to wear down even when red hot. So they go into turbine parts, valve seats and cutting tools.

uses.title: High-temperature magnets
uses.why: Samarium-cobalt and alnico magnets stay magnetic at heat that would weaken ordinary magnets.

uses.title: Sterilization and radiotherapy
uses.why: Cobalt-60 gives off strong gamma rays. They are used to sterilize medical supplies and treat cancer.

bonds.name: Lithium cobalt oxide
bonds.note: The original lithium-ion cathode. Still used in many phone batteries.

bonds.name: Cobalt blue
bonds.note: Stable deep-blue pigment used in ceramics and paint.

bonds.name: Cobalt oxide
bonds.note: Black oxide used to make other cobalt compounds and catalysts.

number.label: Curie temperature, the heat where a magnet stops working. Cobalt's is the highest of any element

source: Mostly a side product of copper and nickel mining. The biggest share comes from the copper belt of central Africa.

lenses.nexus: Cobalt-molybdenum on alumina is the classic catalyst (reaction helper) that strips sulfur out of refinery streams with hydrogen (hydrodesulfurization). Cobalt also drives low-temperature Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, building long waxy chains from syngas.

name: Nickel
tagline: The hydrogen-handling metal: tough stainless, superalloys, and the Sabatier catalyst.
atomStory: Nickel usually gives up 2 electrons (Ni2+), and its 3d layer is 8 of 10 full. On a nickel surface, those d electrons can grab an H2 molecule and split it into two H atoms. Then nickel passes them to other molecules. That is why nickel is a top helper (catalyst) for adding hydrogen. In steel, it holds iron in a crystal pattern that stays tough when frozen.

uses.title: Stainless steel
uses.why: About 8% nickel locks iron into a crystal form called austenite. It stays bendy instead of brittle at super-cold (cryogenic) temperatures, and it is not magnetic.

uses.title: Superalloys
uses.why: Nickel alloys like Inconel stay strong near 1,000 °C. Tiny Ni3Al specks stop the metal from bending out of shape. So they are used in jet turbines and rocket engine parts.

uses.title: Batteries
uses.why: High-nickel cathodes (NMC, NCA) store more energy per kilogram. Nickel shifts between charges as lithium moves in and out.

uses.title: Hydrogenation catalysts
uses.why: Nickel adds hydrogen to double bonds, where two atoms hold two hands at once. It turns vegetable oils into solid fats and upgrades refinery streams.

bonds.name: Nickel oxide
bonds.note: Green-black oxide. The form of nickel in many catalysts before hydrogen switches them on.

bonds.name: Nickel carbonyl
bonds.note: A very toxic gas used to purify nickel (the Mond process). Make the gas, then heat it to leave pure metal behind.

bonds.name: Nickel aluminide
bonds.note: The strengthening specks inside nickel superalloys.

number.label: Nickel in 304 stainless steel (with ~18% chromium). Enough to keep it tough at super-cold temperatures

source: Mined from sulfide ores like pentlandite, including Canada's Sudbury basin, an ancient meteorite crater. Also from laterite ores formed by tropical weathering.

lenses.nexus: Nickel catalysts (reaction helpers) run steam methane reforming, which makes hydrogen. They also run the Sabatier reaction (CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O). Nickel-molybdenum catalysts treat oils with hydrogen, including upgrading pyrolysis oil.
lenses.rocket: SpaceX's Mars plan is to make methane propellant with the Sabatier reaction on a nickel catalyst. It would use CO2 from the air and hydrogen from water ice. Nickel superalloys handle the hottest oxygen-rich engine parts. Raptor reportedly uses an in-house nickel superalloy.

name: Copper
tagline: The wiring metal: one loose outer electron makes it a cheap, great conductor.
atomStory: Copper's inner 3d layer is completely full at 10. That leaves one electron alone in its outer 4s layer, loosely held behind 28 others. In solid copper, every atom lets that electron go into a shared sea of electrons. Push with a voltage and the sea drifts. That drift is an electric current.

uses.title: Electrical wiring
uses.why: Each atom adds its one loose 4s electron to the sea. Copper's neat crystal lets them flow without bumping much. Only silver conducts better, and copper costs far less.

uses.title: Motors and transformers
uses.why: Copper coils carry high current and waste little as heat. So motors and transformers run more efficiently.

uses.title: Heat exchangers
uses.why: The same free electrons carry heat. Copper's thermal conductivity is about 400 W/m·K, roughly 25 times stainless steel's. Used in radiators, heat sinks and rocket chambers.

uses.title: Plumbing
uses.why: Copper reacts far less than iron, so pipes corrode slowly instead of rusting through. Dissolved copper ions (charged copper atoms) also hold back germs.

bonds.name: Copper oxides
bonds.note: The red and black tarnish that forms when copper gets hot or ages in air.

bonds.name: Copper sulfate
bonds.note: Bright blue salt used in copper-refining baths and to kill fungus.

bonds.name: Basic copper carbonate (malachite)
bonds.note: Green mineral, and part of the green coat on old copper roofs.

bonds.name: Brass and bronze
bonds.note: Copper mixed with zinc (brass) or tin (bronze). Harder than pure copper, and bronze named an age of history.

number.label: How well it carries electricity (conductivity), second only to silver

source: Mined mostly from chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) in huge, low-grade porphyry deposits. Then it is smelted and cleaned up with electricity to 99.99% pure.

lenses.nexus: Copper-zinc oxide catalysts (reaction helpers) make methanol from syngas. They also run the low-temperature water-gas shift, which turns CO and steam into hydrogen.
lenses.rocket: Engines cooled by their own fuel line the burn chamber with copper alloys. Copper pulls heat into the cooling channels fastest. The Shuttle's RS-25 used a copper-silver-zirconium alloy. NASA developed copper-chromium-niobium GRCop alloys. Raptor's chamber is reported to be copper alloy too.

name: Zinc
tagline: The sacrificial metal: it corrodes first so steel doesn't.
atomStory: Zinc's 3d layer is completely full, so those electrons stay out of bonding. Zinc simply gives up its 2 outer electrons to become Zn2+, the only charge it takes. That makes it act more like magnesium than iron. Its atoms also hold each other weakly, so it melts low for a transition metal.

uses.title: Galvanizing steel
uses.why: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron. So a zinc coat corrodes first and protects the steel under it, even at scratches. About half of all zinc goes to this.

uses.title: Brass
uses.why: Mixing zinc into copper makes brass. It is harder than pure copper and easier to machine.

uses.title: Batteries
uses.why: Zinc metal is the - end (anode) in alkaline and zinc-air batteries. Each atom gives up 2 electrons as it reacts.

uses.title: Rubber and sunscreen
uses.why: Zinc oxide gets the sulfur links going when tires are cured (vulcanized). In sunscreen, it soaks up UV light.

bonds.name: Zinc oxide
bonds.note: White powder used in tires, sunscreen, and beds that clean gas.

bonds.name: Zinc sulfide
bonds.note: Sphalerite, the main zinc ore. Also a glow-in-the-dark material.

number.label: Melting point. Low for a transition metal, because its full 3d layer adds little to bonding

source: Mined as sphalerite (ZnS) and roasted into zinc oxide. Then it is dissolved and cleaned up with electricity, or smelted.

lenses.nexus: Tires have about 1-2% zinc oxide from curing. When tires are pyrolyzed, most of it ends up in the char. In gas plants and refineries, beds of zinc oxide soak up H2S and turn into zinc sulfide.

name: Gallium
tagline: The metal that melts in your hand. It has 3 hands and an oddly loose crystal.
atomStory: Gallium sits right under aluminum and has the same 3 hands. It can share its 3 outer electrons or give them away, so it makes 3 bonds. In solid gallium, atoms pair up loosely instead of packing tight like most metals. So it melts at about 30 °C but does not boil until about 2,400 °C. Like water, it gets bigger when it freezes.

uses.title: LEDs and chips (GaN, GaAs)
uses.why: Gallium joined with nitrogen or arsenic makes a crystal where electrons (tiny charged bits of atoms) jump a set energy step and give off one color of light. Gallium nitride made bright blue and white LEDs possible.

uses.title: Space solar cells
uses.why: Gallium-based layers are stacked, and each one catches a different slice of sunlight. Together they turn more of it into power than plain silicon. Power per kilogram matters most on satellites.

uses.title: Liquid-metal thermometers (Galinstan)
uses.why: A mix of gallium, indium and tin stays liquid down to about -19 °C. It replaces mercury because it is far less poisonous.

uses.title: Fast power electronics
uses.why: Gallium nitride switches (transistors) handle high voltage and flip very fast while wasting little energy. That is why phone chargers using them are smaller.

bonds.name: Gallium arsenide
bonds.note: A semiconductor (a material that only partly conducts, so it can act as a switch). Ga brings 3 outer electrons and As brings 5, an average of 4 each, like silicon. Used in lasers, radio chips and space solar cells.

bonds.name: Gallium nitride
bonds.note: A hard semiconductor with a wide energy step. It is behind blue LEDs and small power chargers.

bonds.name: Trimethylgallium
bonds.note: The gallium cousin of triethylaluminum. It catches fire in air. Chip factories use it as the gallium source when growing GaN and GaAs layers.

number.label: Melting point, below body temperature

source: Collected as a leftover when making alumina (aluminum oxide) from bauxite ore. A smaller amount comes from zinc refining.

lenses.rocket: Many satellites, especially high-power ones, run on stacked (multi-junction) solar cells. The layers are gallium-indium-phosphide and gallium-arsenide on a germanium wafer. They turn about 30% of sunlight into power, versus about 20% for good silicon.

name: Germanium
tagline: Silicon's bigger sibling. It made the first transistors and now makes infrared lenses.
atomStory: Germanium has 4 hands, like carbon and silicon. So it holds hands with 4 neighbors in a diamond-shaped crystal. Its atom is bigger than silicon's, so its outer electrons are held more loosely and break free more easily. That makes it a semiconductor with a smaller energy step. When hot, it lets current through too easily.

uses.title: Infrared optics
uses.why: Because its energy step is small, long-wave infrared (heat light) passes right through it, while visible light is blocked. Thermal cameras and night-sight lenses are made of it.

uses.title: Fiber-optic cable
uses.why: A little germanium oxide in the glass core makes it bend light more. So light bounces along the core instead of leaking out.

uses.title: Solar cell wafers for space
uses.why: Its atoms are spaced almost the same as in gallium arsenide. So the high-efficiency cell layers can grow cleanly on top of it.

uses.title: The first transistors
uses.why: The 1947 Bell Labs transistor was germanium. Silicon replaced it because germanium parts leaked current as they warmed up.

bonds.name: Germanium dioxide
bonds.note: A glass-like oxide. Used in fiber cores and as a catalyst (a helper that speeds a reaction without being used up) for some PET plastic.

bonds.name: Germanium tetrachloride
bonds.note: A liquid that turns to gas easily. It is burned with oxygen to lay GeO2 into fiber-optic glass. It is also the main way germanium is purified.

bonds.name: Germane
bonds.note: Germanium's version of methane: one Ge holding 4 hydrogens. Chip makers use this gas to lay down germanium.

number.label: Energy step (band gap), vs about 1.1 eV for silicon

source: Collected as a leftover from refining zinc ore and from some coal fly ash.

lenses.nexus: Antimony is the usual catalyst for making PET plastic. Germanium dioxide is used for some clearer, higher-grade bottle plastic.
lenses.rocket: Germanium wafers are the base layer of the stacked solar cells on many satellites. The bottom germanium layer also catches the infrared the upper layers miss.

name: Arsenic
tagline: The classic poison. It also tunes semiconductors, because it looks like phosphorus.
atomStory: Arsenic has 5 outer electrons but 3 hands, just like phosphorus right above it. That likeness is the problem. Arsenate slips into spots in cells meant for phosphate and jams the chemistry that makes energy. In a silicon crystal, arsenic uses 4 electrons to hold hands and has 1 left over to carry current.

uses.title: Doping silicon (n-type)
uses.why: Each arsenic atom in silicon holds hands with 4 neighbors. Its 5th electron is free to move, adding extra negative charge carriers.

uses.title: Gallium arsenide chips
uses.why: Joined with gallium, it makes a fast semiconductor. It is used in radio chips, lasers and space solar cells.

uses.title: Hardening lead
uses.why: A little arsenic makes lead harder and helps melted lead form round drops. This is used in lead shot and some battery grids.

uses.title: Leukemia treatment
uses.why: Arsenic trioxide is an approved drug for one type of leukemia (a blood cancer). At a controlled dose, its poison is aimed at cancer cells.

bonds.name: Arsenic trioxide
bonds.note: The old 'white arsenic' poison and a modern cancer drug. It is also the main form sold.

bonds.name: Arsine
bonds.note: Arsenic's version of ammonia: 3 hydrogens holding its 3 hands. An extremely toxic gas chip factories use to add arsenic to silicon.

bonds.name: Gallium arsenide
bonds.note: The semiconductor where arsenic's 5 outer electrons and gallium's 3 average out to 4, like silicon.

number.label: At normal pressure it skips liquid and turns straight to gas (sublimes)

source: Collected as a leftover from copper and lead smelting, mostly from the mineral arsenopyrite (FeAsS).

lenses.nexus: Tiny amounts of arsenic in crude oil and naphtha poison refinery catalysts. Arsine in propylene streams poisons the catalysts that link it into plastic. So plants run guard beds (filters) to strip it out.

name: Selenium
tagline: Sulfur's heavier cousin. It conducts better in light, and a tiny bit is a nutrient that turns toxic.
atomStory: Selenium has 6 outer electrons but 2 hands, like oxygen and sulfur above it. It is bigger, so its outer electrons are held more loosely. Light can knock them free to carry current. That is why it conducts much better when light hits it.

uses.title: Glass color control
uses.why: Selenium adds a faint pink that cancels the green tint iron gives glass. More of it makes red glass.

uses.title: Early photocopiers and light meters
uses.why: Light frees electrons in selenium, so a lit spot loses its static charge. Xerox machines used selenium drums to make the image.

uses.title: Thin-film solar cells (CIGS)
uses.why: Copper indium gallium selenide soaks up sunlight strongly, even in a very thin layer.

uses.title: Nutrition
uses.why: The body builds selenium into a few enzymes (helper proteins) that protect cells from oxidation damage. Too much is toxic.

bonds.name: Hydrogen selenide
bonds.note: Selenium's version of water and H2S: 2 hydrogens holding its 2 hands. A foul-smelling, toxic gas.

bonds.name: Zinc selenide
bonds.note: Infrared light passes through it, so it is used for windows and lenses in CO2 lasers.

bonds.name: Cadmium selenide
bonds.note: Made as tiny crystals (quantum dots). Their color depends on their size.

number.label: Daily need for US adults; the safe upper limit is 400 µg

source: Collected from the sludge left over when copper is purified with electricity (electrolysis).

name: Bromine
tagline: A red-brown liquid halogen. It stops flames by grabbing the radicals (atoms with an empty hand) that feed them.
atomStory: Bromine has 7 outer electrons and 1 hand. Two bromine atoms hold hands to form Br2. It is bigger than chlorine, so Br2 molecules are heavy and cling together. That is why it is a liquid at room temperature. Its one empty hand makes it reactive, but less so than chlorine above it.

uses.title: Flame retardants
uses.why: When plastic heats up, bromine compounds release bromine. It grabs the H and OH radicals that keep a flame's chain reaction going.

uses.title: Oil and gas drilling brines
uses.why: Calcium and zinc bromide dissolve into very heavy, clear liquids. These hold back the pressure in a well without any solids.

uses.title: Pool and spa disinfection
uses.why: Bromine compounds kill germs like chlorine does but hold up better in hot water.

uses.title: Halon fire suppression
uses.why: Halon 1301 (CBrF3) puts out fires the same way, by grabbing radicals. It was mostly phased out for harming the ozone layer, except in aviation.

bonds.name: Bromine
bonds.note: Two atoms holding hands, filling each other's last empty hand. A heavy, toxic red-brown liquid.

bonds.name: Hydrogen bromide
bonds.note: A strong acid gas. It is what a burning flame retardant releases to stop the fire.

bonds.name: Calcium bromide
bonds.note: A salt that makes the heavy brines (salty water) used to finish oil and gas wells.

bonds.name: Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA)
bonds.note: One of the most common flame retardants. It is built into circuit-board plastic.

number.label: Melting point. With mercury, one of only two elements liquid at room temperature

source: Pulled from salty water, like the Dead Sea and underground brines in Arkansas. Chlorine is bubbled in. It takes bromide's extra electron and frees Br2.

lenses.nexus: Flame retardants in electronics plastics carry bromine into pyrolysis. There it forms HBr and bromine-laced oils that eat away equipment and spoil the product. So plants like Nexus usually keep this feed out or treat it first.

name: Krypton
tagline: A heavy noble gas, used where argon is too light and xenon costs too much.
atomStory: Krypton's outer ring is full at 8, so it has 0 hands and almost never bonds. It is bigger than argon, so its outer electrons are a little easier to pull. That lets fluorine force it into a few rare compounds. Its heavy atoms move slowly, so they carry heat poorly.

uses.title: Insulated windows
uses.why: Heavy, slow krypton atoms carry heat across the narrow gap between panes worse than air or argon do.

uses.title: Lighting
uses.why: As a fill gas, it slows a hot tungsten filament from boiling away. It also gives some flash and specialty lamps their light.

uses.title: Chip lithography lasers
